# Session 5: Advanced Database Search & Profile Methods

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Profile drift

> PSI-BLAST is like social media: after a few iterations, everything it finds agrees with it.
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to:

- explain why exact dynamic programming does not scale to searching a
  whole database;
- describe BLAST's seed-extend-evaluate heuristic, and how MMseqs2
  scales the same ideas;
- interpret the E-value and bit score of a real BLAST result;
- construct a small position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM) by hand, and
  explain why pseudocounts matter;
- describe PSI-BLAST as BLAST iterated with a PSSM instead of a single
  sequence, and explain why iteration can drift;
- explain, at a conceptual level, what a profile Hidden Markov Model
  adds beyond a PSSM.

## The scaling problem, and BLAST's heuristic answer

Session 4's dynamic programming finds the *provably optimal* alignment
between two sequences, but its cost is proportional to the product of
their lengths. For two sequences a few hundred residues long, this is no
problem. For searching one query against a database, it is. GenBank and
UniProt hold well over a hundred million sequences between them, and
running full dynamic programming against every entry would take far too
long to be useful. A database search therefore needs a faster method.

**BLAST** (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) is such a method, and it
trades the guarantee of optimality for speed. Instead of filling a DP
matrix for every database sequence, it first looks for short exact or
near-exact matches. Only the promising regions that these matches point
to get the expensive alignment step. Concretely, BLAST runs in three
stages:

1. **Seeding.** Break the query into short "words", list every word that
   scores well against each of them, and scan the database for
   occurrences of those words.
2. **Extension.** Grow each seed hit outwards, in both directions, into
   a full local alignment.
3. **Evaluation.** Ask whether the score of the resulting alignment is
   better than what pure chance would produce.

Each stage is covered in its own section below. This three-stage picture
is the core idea, and it is deliberately simplified. Production BLAST
adds refinements such as the *two-hit* rule (only extend when two seeds
lie close together on the same diagonal), masking of low-complexity
regions, gapped extension, and corrections for unusual amino-acid
composition. None of these refinements changes the logic of seed,
extend, evaluate.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [BLAST (biotechnology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLAST_(biotechnology))
- NCBI, [BLAST Help](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1762/) — the practical reference for choosing blastp/blastn/blastx and reading real output

## Stage 1: seeding — turning the query into fast lookups

The first stage turns the query into a set of short words. For protein
sequences, a "word" is usually only 3 residues long, so a query of
length 200 has 198 overlapping 3-letter words. BLAST does not search the
database only for *exact* matches to these words, because a biologically
real match may substitute a residue or two without losing significance.
Instead, it uses a substitution matrix (BLOSUM62, from Session 4) to
precompute every 3-letter combination that scores *above a threshold*
$T$ against each query word.

**Worked example.** Scored with the real BLOSUM62 matrix, several other
words besides the query word `LWG` itself clear a typical threshold of
$T=12$. The notebook computes them directly from BLOSUM62, and 49 words
clear the threshold in total. The top ones are:

| Neighbour word | Score vs. `LWG` |
|---|---|
| `LWG` | 21 |
| `IWG` | 19 |
| `MWG` | 19 |
| `VWG` | 18 |
| `FWG` | 17 |
| `AWG` | 16 |
| `CWG` | 16 |
| `TWG` | 16 |
| `YWG` | 16 |
| `KWG` | 15 |

: The highest-scoring neighbour words of the query word `LWG`. {#tbl-s05-neighbours}

These query words and their high-scoring neighbours go into a **lookup
table**, which is built once per query and records, for every 3-letter
word, which query positions it would seed. BLAST then scans each
database sequence once, from start to end. For every 3-letter word it
reads, it asks the table "does this word seed anything in the query, and
where?" Because that check is a single table lookup, the scan is fast
and linear in the size of the database. Only the few places that produce
a seed go on to the expensive extension step.

## Stage 2: extension — growing a seed into a real alignment

A seed hit is only a 3-letter coincidence and not yet evidence of
anything. BLAST therefore extends it outwards in both directions and
recomputes a running score as it goes. The scoring uses the same
substitution-matrix logic as Session 4's dynamic programming, but
without filling a full matrix. Instead, extension stops as soon as the
running score has fallen too far below its own best point so far.

**The X-drop rule.** BLAST tracks the *running score* as the alignment
extends, and separately the *best score seen so far*. If the running
score ever falls more than a threshold $X$ below that best score, the
alignment is very unlikely to recover, so extension stops. The reported
alignment is then trimmed back to the point where the best score
occurred.

**Worked example**, adapted from Korf, Yandell & Bedell (2003). We treat
two short strings as if they were sequences, score $+1$ for a matching
character and $-1$ for a mismatch (ignoring spaces), and use $X=5$:

```
query:    Thequickbrownfoxjumps...
database: Thequietbrownncatpurrs...
```

The running score climbs steadily through `Thequ`, dips slightly at the
`ick`/`iet` mismatch, and then recovers and climbs further through
`brown` to a peak of **9** right after `...brown`/`...brown`. After that
it falls steadily, as `foxjump` diverges from `catpurr`. Once the
running score has dropped 5 points below the peak of 9, extension stops.
The reported alignment is trimmed back to the peak itself, so it pairs
`Thequickbrown` with `Thequietbrown` and leaves out the lower-scoring
tail beyond it. The notebook reproduces this computation in code.

## Stage 3: is this hit significant? E-values and bit scores

Extending every seed produces a raw alignment score. A raw score alone,
however, does not say whether the alignment is *meaningful* or simply
what we would expect from two random sequences of that length. To
decide, we need to know how scores are distributed by chance. Karlin and
Altschul proved in 1990 that the scores from aligning a query against
random sequence data follow an **extreme value (Gumbel) distribution**,
not a normal distribution, and this result underpins BLAST's statistics.

From that distribution follows the expected number of alignments that
score at least $S$ purely by chance, the **E-value**:

$$
E = K m n\, e^{-\lambda S}
$$

Here $m$ and $n$ are the lengths of the query and the database, and $K$
and $\lambda$ are constants of the particular scoring system
(substitution matrix and gap penalties), which real BLAST output reports
as "Karlin-Altschul statistics". This is the simplified textbook form.
Real BLAST replaces $m$ and $n$ by slightly smaller *effective* lengths
(an alignment cannot start right at the end of a sequence) and adjusts
for composition, but the behaviour is the same.

Two consequences of the formula matter. First, a higher score gives an
exponentially smaller $E$. Second, a bigger database ($n$) inflates $E$
for the *same* alignment, because chance has more opportunities to
produce a false hit. An E-value is therefore only meaningful together
with the database it was computed against, and the same alignment can be
"significant" against a small database but not against all of GenBank.

Raw scores and E-values both depend on the scoring system, which makes
them awkward to compare across different searches. The **bit score**
solves this by normalising away the scoring system:

$$
S' = \frac{\lambda S - \ln K}{\ln 2}
$$

Bit scores from completely different searches, even ones that use
different substitution matrices, can therefore be compared directly. A
bit score is not a significance test on its own, though. There is no
universal bit-score cutoff, because whether a given score is surprising
still depends on the size of the search space it was found in. For
significance, read the E-value.

**Reading real output.** A real local BLASTP search of *HBB*
(beta-globin, `P68871`) against its five closest human globin relatives
gives the following hits:

| Hit | % identity | E-value | Bit score |
|---|---|---|---|
| Delta-globin (`HBD`) | 93.2% | 9.3×10⁻¹⁰⁵ | 284 |
| Epsilon-globin (`HBE`) | 75.5% | 2.1×10⁻⁸⁷ | 240 |
| Alpha-globin (`HBA`) | 43.4% | 9.0×10⁻³⁸ | 114 |
| Zeta-globin (`HBAZ`) | 35.9% | 3.8×10⁻³² | 100 |
| Myoglobin (`MYG`) | 16.0% | 63 | 10.8 |

: A local BLASTP search of *HBB* against its five closest human globin relatives. {#tbl-s05-hbb-hits}

The first four are all confident, high-quality hits, with high percent
identity, astronomically small E-values and comfortably high bit scores.
Myoglobin is the interesting case. It shares the globin fold and a real
evolutionary origin with haemoglobin, yet BLAST reports only a weak
alignment with an E-value of 63, which taken at face value is no
statistical evidence at all. That number, however, only evaluates the
alignment BLAST *found*. If we run the same search with the two-hit rule
switched off (so that every single seed gets extended; `-window_size 0`
in BLAST+), BLAST finds a full-length alignment, 145 residues at 25.5%
identity, with an E-value of 5×10⁻¹¹. With the default settings, no pair
of seeds happened to fall close enough together on the right diagonal,
so the good alignment was never extended. This is the price of a
heuristic. BLAST is fast because it skips most of the search, and
occasionally it skips the answer, which an optimal Smith–Waterman search
would not have missed.

Database size still matters as well. These E-values are relative to a
tiny five-sequence database. Against a database the size of UniProtKB
(about $9\times10^{10}$ residues), the same full-length myoglobin
alignment would get an E-value of about 0.007, which is significant, but
only just. Relatives that have diverged further than myoglobin, such as
the bacterial *truncated* haemoglobins, give no detectable pairwise
signal at all, even with the optimal alignment (Session 6 shows that
they still share the globin fold).

### Further reading

- Original source: Karlin & Altschul (1990), *PNAS* 87:2264-2268 — the full derivation behind the formula above

## BLAST's ideas at modern database scale: MMseqs2

BLAST was designed in 1990, when the protein databases held tens of
thousands of sequences. Today's metagenomic collections hold billions,
and at that scale even BLAST becomes too slow. **MMseqs2** (Steinegger &
Söding, 2017) is a widely used modern search tool that keeps BLAST's
logic but turns one part of it around. In simplified form, it works as
follows:

1. **Index the target database by short words** (k-mers, typically 6–7
   residues for proteins). The index is a table that maps each k-mer to
   the database sequences and positions where it occurs, and it is built
   once and reused.
2. For each k-mer in the query, generate the **similar** k-mers (scored
   with a substitution matrix, exactly like BLAST's neighbour words) and
   look them up in the index.
3. Keep only database sequences in which **two matching k-mers fall on
   the same diagonal**, that is, at the same offset between query and
   target position, just as in a dot plot from Session 4. Two consistent
   hits are much stronger evidence of a real alignment than one.
4. Score the surviving candidates quickly with an **ungapped alignment**
   along that diagonal, and discard the weak ones.
5. Run the expensive **gapped Smith–Waterman** alignment, heavily
   optimised to use the processor's vector instructions, only on the
   small set that is left.

The difference from classic BLAST lies in which side gets indexed. BLAST
builds a lookup table from the *query* and its neighbour words, and then
reads through every database sequence. MMseqs2 instead indexes the
*database* once, so each query only has to look up its own k-mers. Steps
3–5 form a cascade of ever more expensive filters, each of which passes
on only a small fraction of the candidates. As a result, MMseqs2 is
often hundreds of times faster than BLAST at similar sensitivity. No
machine learning is involved, because MMseqs2 simply engineers the same
seed-extend-evaluate ideas for scale.

Like PSI-BLAST below, MMseqs2 can also iterate, turning its hits into a
profile and searching again, and ColabFold uses it to build the
alignments that AlphaFold needs (Session 12). Session 6 meets its
structural counterpart, Foldseek, from the same group.

## From one sequence to many: PSI-BLAST and the PSSM

Myoglobin sits near the edge of what a single sequence can detect, and
more distant relatives lie beyond it. The reason is that ordinary BLAST
scores everything against one fixed substitution matrix, whatever family
the query belongs to, so a faint but real family signal is easily lost
against the background of a large database. **PSI-BLAST**
(Position-Specific Iterated BLAST) does better, because it builds a
*query-specific* scoring matrix and refines it over several rounds:

1. Run an ordinary BLAST search with the query sequence.
2. Take the hits that pass the **inclusion threshold** (an E-value
   cutoff, by default stricter than the one used for *reporting* hits),
   align them to the query, and turn that alignment into a
   **position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM)**, described below. Hits
   that are displayed but fall short of the inclusion threshold do not
   enter the profile.
3. Search the database again, this time scoring with the PSSM instead of
   a generic substitution matrix.
4. Repeat, so that each round's included hits refine the PSSM further,
   until no new sequences pass the threshold (convergence) or a set
   number of rounds is reached.

This makes PSI-BLAST more sensitive than a single BLAST pass,
particularly for *remote* homologs whose similarity to the original
query is too faint for a fixed substitution matrix to catch.

**Iteration is not automatically better: profile drift.** Suppose that
one unrelated sequence passes the inclusion threshold. It then enters
the alignment and shifts the next PSSM a little towards itself. The next
round finds more sequences like the intruder, which shift the profile
further. After a few rounds, the "family" can be dominated by proteins
that have nothing to do with the original query, often through a shared
low-complexity or coiled-coil region rather than real homology. This is
a general lesson that returns in the machine-learning half of the
course. A model is only as good as the examples it was built from, and a
model that chooses its own training data can reinforce its own mistakes.
In practice, keep the inclusion threshold strict, look at what entered
in each round, and check surprising late-round hits independently.

### Building a PSSM, step by step

Session 4 ended with alignment columns, their entropy, and sequence
logos. A logo *describes* an alignment column, whereas a PSSM turns the
same column statistics into numbers that can *score* a new sequence. The
recipe below is a teaching model. The real PSI-BLAST computation also
weights the sequences and uses more sophisticated pseudocounts, as noted
along the way, but every step serves the same purpose in the real thing.

**1. Count.** From a multiple sequence alignment, count how often each
residue appears at each position. Take this small toy alignment of 5
sequences:

```
Position:   1 2 3 4 5
Protein 1:  A G L S P
Protein 2:  A G L T P
Protein 3:  R G I S P
Protein 4:  A A L S Q
Protein 5:  A A L S P
```

At position 1, 4 of the 5 sequences have `A` and 1 has `R`. At position
5, 4 have `P` and 1 has `Q`, and so on.

Real alignments are rarely this balanced. If a search returns fifty
nearly identical mammalian sequences and three distant ones, raw counts
would make the profile describe mammals rather than the family. Real
tools therefore **reduce redundancy or weight sequences**, removing or
down-weighting near-duplicates so that an over-represented subfamily
does not dominate the counts. The exact recipe varies between programs,
but the principle is what matters.

**2. Add pseudocounts.** Turning raw counts straight into frequencies
causes two problems. First, a residue that never appears at a position
gets a frequency of exactly zero, and its log-odds score becomes
$-\infty$. Second, with only 5 sequences, the absence of a residue might
be bad luck rather than a real biological signal. **Pseudocounts**,
small constants added to every count before the frequencies are
computed, solve both problems. In our teaching model we add $+1$
uniformly to the count of every residue type at every position.
Conceptually, a pseudocount is a **prior**, that is, what we assume
about a column before looking at the alignment (here, "every residue is
possible"). With only five sequences the prior has a large influence,
while with hundreds of sequences the observed counts swamp it. Real
tools use smarter priors, for example by giving larger pseudocounts to
residues that substitute easily for the observed ones (according to a
substitution matrix).

**3. Compare to background.** Compute each residue's **background
frequency** $q_j$, that is, how often it occurs in proteins generally
(e.g. alanine ≈7.4%, tryptophan ≈1.3%), independently of this alignment.

**4. Compute log-odds scores.** For each position $i$ and residue $j$,

$$
S_{i,j} = \log_2 \frac{f_{i,j}}{q_j}
$$

Here $f_{i,j}$ is the (pseudocount-adjusted) observed frequency. With
base 2, a score of $+1$ means "twice as likely here as by chance", $+3$
means "8× as likely", and so on. Arranged into a matrix, with one row
per alignment position and one column per residue, the scores $S_{i,j}$
*are* the PSSM. (Some tools store the matrix the other way round, but
the orientation is only a storage convention.) Scoring a candidate
sequence against the PSSM means looking up one value per position and
**summing** them. This is the weighted-sum, or dot-product, idea from
Session 1, generalised to sequence positions.

The notebook builds this PSSM from the alignment above and confirms that
the highest-scoring sequence the matrix can produce is `AGLSP`, the
alignment's own consensus, as it should be.

**Why pseudocounts really matter.** With only five sequences, every
frequency is a small-sample estimate, and the raw log-odds score takes
it at face value. Take a position where 4 of 5 sequences show alanine
(background 7.4%) and 1 shows the much rarer tryptophan (1.3%). The raw
scores are $\log_2(0.8/0.074) \approx 3.43$ for alanine and
$\log_2(0.2/0.013) \approx 3.94$ for tryptophan, so a single observation
outscores four. Yet one tryptophan in five sequences could easily be
chance, and the score treats it as a reliable frequency of 20%. With
$+1$ pseudocounts the frequencies become 5/25 and 2/25, and the scores
fall to 1.43 and 2.62. The pseudocounts make every score more cautious,
but they do not change the ranking: tryptophan still wins. A pseudocount
cannot tell a lucky single observation from a real one; only more
sequences can.

**Gaps.** A PSSM contains only substitution scores, one row per
position. To align a new sequence to it, PSI-BLAST therefore uses
ordinary gapped alignment, the same dynamic programming as in Session 4,
with the PSSM row for position $i$ taking the place of the
substitution-matrix row for query residue $i$. The gap-open and
gap-extension penalties are the ordinary ones, the same at every
position.

**A PSSM is already a linear model.** For an ungapped sequence
$x = x_1 x_2 \dots x_L$, the PSSM score is

$$
S(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{L} w[i, x_i],
$$

where $w[i, x_i]$ is the matrix entry for residue $x_i$ at position $i$.
The score is thus one weight looked up per position and added up.
Session 7 keeps this weighted-sum idea but *learns* the weights from
labelled examples instead of deriving them from alignment counts.

## Profile Hidden Markov Models: what a PSSM still can't represent

A PSSM gives position-specific *substitution* scores, but the alignment
algorithm handles gaps separately, with the same penalties everywhere.
Real families are not like that. A loop between two helices may tolerate
insertions of any length, while the core of the domain almost never has
one. A **profile Hidden Markov Model (profile HMM)** therefore
integrates position-specific match, insertion and deletion behaviour
into one probabilistic model of the family. It uses three kinds of
states, arranged in a repeating unit with one unit per alignment
position:

- **Match (M)** states represent a conserved position. Each has its own
  per-residue emission probabilities and plays the same role as one
  column of a PSSM.
- **Insert (I)** states represent extra residues between conserved
  positions. The model can emit a residue from them and then loop back
  to allow more than one.
- **Delete (D)** states represent a skipped conserved position and emit
  nothing at all.

Special **Begin** and **End** states bookend the model. Transitions
connect the M/I/D states of consecutive positions (e.g. $M_i \to
M_{i+1}$, $M_i \to I_i$, $M_i \to D_{i+1}$), and each transition has its
own learned probability.

**Why "hidden".** For an observed residue in a real sequence, the model
never tells you directly whether it came from a Match state or an Insert
state. That has to be *inferred* from the path through the states that
best explains the whole sequence, using the emission and transition
probabilities together. The states generate what you observe, but they
themselves stay hidden.

This is the extra structure that PSSMs lack, and it is why profile HMMs,
not PSSMs, are the standard tool behind large-scale protein family
databases such as **Pfam**. A profile HMM trained on a protein family
can recognise a new sequence as a member even when it has a genuinely
different number of residues in a variable region. The model itself has
learned *where* insertions and deletions are common in that family,
which a PSSM with uniform gap penalties can only approximate.

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## What neither a PSSM nor a profile HMM can represent

Both models score a sequence position by position. The score is a sum
over columns, so each position contributes independently of the others.
Real proteins do not always work that way. When mutations interact, so
that the effect of one depends on the residue at another position
(**epistasis**), no profile can capture it. Session 9 shows a protein
where this matters (all 160,000 variants at four positions of GB1), and
Session 12 shows how pairwise models fitted to an alignment (direct
coupling analysis) add those interactions.
:::

## Worked example: a real profile-HMM hit on *HBB*

The same idea works on a real sequence at production scale. To tie this
back to the *HBB* (beta-globin) locus from Session 3, we search Pfam's
library of profile HMMs against the real UniProt entry `P68871`
(HBB_HUMAN), fetched live via EBI's InterPro API. The search finds a
match to **PF00042 ("Globin")**, spanning residues 27-142 of the
147-residue protein, with an E-value of around $1.3\times10^{-29}$. In a
database of this size, essentially no match that good is expected by
chance. The profile HMM thus does on a real sequence what the toy PSSM
above did on paper: it scores how well a sequence matches a family,
position by position.

## The lab

**The full lab** covers BLAST and profile methods as one continuous
exercise. (Session 4 now has its own short lab for alignment practice,
so this one no longer needs to cover alignment as well.) You first
identify a real, unknown gene from a raw sequence through a real NCBI
BLAST search. It turns out to be a sixth real human globin-family gene,
continuing this course's running thread. Three code exercises follow: a
real ClustalW alignment and PSSM on five globin-family proteins, a real
PSI-BLAST search that compares its first iteration with its third
against a real local copy of the PDB, and a live Pfam domain search for
HIV-1's Gag-Pol polyprotein via the same InterPro API that this page's
HBB worked example uses.

**We recommend running this lab on the shared course server**, not only
in Colab, because the bioinformatics tools it uses (`clustalw`,
`psiblast`) are real command-line programs. On Colab the lab notebook
installs them first, while on the course server they are already
installed. Running them over an SSH connection (see Session 2's
"Connecting to the shared course server") is also a transferable skill
in its own right. Once you are connected via VS Code, either open
[`notebooks/session05-lab.ipynb`](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/session05-lab.ipynb)
there directly (VS Code's Jupyter support runs it on the server, not on
your laptop), or open a terminal alongside it and run the same commands
by hand. Colab still works if you do not have server access set up yet,
since it is the same lab notebook either way.

### Submitting this lab

This lab is administered through Canvas, not through this book. See the
course's Canvas page for the current quiz, the deadline and how to
submit.

## What's next

A remote homolog can become impossible to recognise from its sequence
while its fold stays conserved. Session 6 therefore turns to structure:
the four levels of protein structure, explored hands-on in PyMOL,
structure alignment, and structural search with Foldseek. Session 7 then
returns to the weighted sum $S(x) = \sum_i w[i, x_i]$ that a PSSM
computes. It formalises the sum as a **perceptron** and shows that its
weights can be *learned* from labelled examples by gradient descent,
instead of being derived from alignment statistics as this session's
PSSM was.
